organism: Bordetella pertussis, a small aerobic gram-negative rod requiring special media for isolation. It produces several antigenic and biologically active products - pertussis toxin, filamentous hemagglutinin, agglutinogens, adenylate cyclase, pertactin, and tracheal cytotoxin - responsible for the disease's clinical features. Pertussis is primarily a toxin-mediated disease, and immunity after natural infection is not permanent.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Incubation period is commonly 7-10 days (range 4-21). Illness has three stages: catarrhal (1-2 weeks, cold-like symptoms), paroxysmal (1-6 weeks, bursts of rapid coughing often ending in an inspiratory whoop, with possible cyanosis and vomiting), and convalescent (gradual recovery over weeks to months). Infants younger than 6 months may not have the strength to whoop but still have paroxysms. Previously vaccinated adolescents and adults often have milder, sometimes atypical disease but can still transmit it, frequently to unimmunized infants.
epidemiologySummary: Pertussis is a human-only disease with no known animal reservoir; adolescents, adults, and older school-age children are an important reservoir and frequent source of infant infections. Transmission is via respiratory droplets or contact with airborne secretions. There is no distinct seasonal pattern, though cases may rise in summer and fall. It is highly communicable - secondary attack rates reach 80% among susceptible household contacts - and patients are infectious from the catarrhal stage through the third week after paroxysm onset, or until 5 days after starting effective antibiotics.
secularTrendsSummary: Before vaccination, the US averaged about 175,000 reported cases per year (1940-1945). Incidence fell to roughly 2,900 cases per year by 1980-1990, but has been gradually increasing since the late 1980s, with large epidemic peaks since the mid-2000s (48,277 cases in 2012, the most since the mid-1950s) - waning immunity from the shift to acellular vaccines in the 1990s is thought to play a key role. Infants under 1 year continue to have the highest disease rates (72.3 per 100,000 in infants under 6 months in 2018), and a growing share of cases now occurs among fully vaccinated older children and adolescents.
vaccineDescription: Whole-cell pertussis vaccine (as DTP) was licensed in 1948 but is no longer used in the US; it has been replaced by acellular pertussis vaccine combined with diphtheria and tetanus toxoids as DTaP (children under 7) or Tdap (age 7+), and in combination products with IPV, Hib, and/or HepB (Pediarix, Pentacel, Vaxelis, Kinrix, Quadracel). Given by intramuscular injection with aluminum adjuvant.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: Routine childhood DTaP schedule is 3 primary doses at 2, 4, and 6 months plus boosters at 15-18 months and 4-6 years; a single Tdap dose is recommended at age 11-12, and adults who have never received Tdap should get one dose.

supplementalTopics.title: Vaccination During Pregnancy
supplementalTopics.summary: A Tdap dose is recommended during every pregnancy, regardless of prior Tdap history, to maximize passive antibody transfer to the newborn before the infant can be vaccinated (an off-label use). Optimal timing is 27-36 weeks gestation, preferably earlier in that window, though Tdap may be given at any point in pregnancy; if not given during pregnancy, it should be given immediately postpartum.

supplementalTopics.title: Cocooning: Vaccinating Infant Contacts
supplementalTopics.summary: Anyone who has not previously received Tdap and anticipates close contact with an infant under 12 months - parents, siblings, grandparents, child care providers, healthcare personnel - should receive a single Tdap dose, ideally at least 2 weeks before contact begins. Healthcare personnel should receive Tdap as soon as feasible regardless of the interval since their last Td dose.

vaccineEfficacySummary: DTaP efficacy has been estimated at 80%-85% in European and African trials. Tdap vaccines were licensed based on immunogenicity 'bridging' studies (comparable antibody response to DTaP) rather than direct efficacy trials. Antipertussis antibody levels peak within a month of a Tdap dose and decline substantially within a year, which is why a single dose during one pregnancy is not assumed to protect a later pregnancy.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose, or encephalopathy within 7 days of a prior DTaP/Tdap dose not attributable to another cause, is a contraindication. Precautions include moderate or severe acute illness, a progressive or unstable neurological disorder, uncontrolled seizures, progressive encephalopathy, Guillain-Barre syndrome within 6 weeks of a prior tetanus toxoid-containing dose, and a history of an Arthus-type reaction to a prior diphtheria- or tetanus toxoid-containing dose (defer at least 10 years in that case).
vaccineSafetySummary: Local reactions (pain, redness, or swelling) are common: 20%-40% of DTaP recipients per dose, and 21%-75% of Tdap/Td recipients, generally self-limited. Temperature of 101F or higher occurs in 3%-5% of DTaP recipients. Moderate or severe systemic reactions occur in fewer than 1 in 10,000 doses. Post-licensure VAERS/VSD surveillance has not shown concerning patterns for either DTaP or Tdap.
vaccineStorageSummary: DTaP and Tdap must be stored at refrigerator temperature, 2C to 8C (36F to 46F). See CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for complete guidance.
surveillanceSummary: Diagnosis relies on clinical history plus culture, PCR, and/or serology, each most useful at different points after cough onset (culture and PCR earliest, serology later). See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for state/local reporting guidance.
keyPoints: Outbreaks first described in the 16th century; B. pertussis was first isolated in 1906

Before vaccination, more than 200,000 US cases were reported annually; pertussis remains a major global problem (an estimated 24 million cases and 160,700 deaths among children under 5 worldwide in 2014)
US incidence has been rising since the late 1980s, with large epidemic peaks since the mid-2000s, likely reflecting waning immunity from acellular vaccines
Secondary bacterial pneumonia is the most common cause of pertussis death; infants under 2 months account for the large majority of deaths
Tdap during every pregnancy (27-36 weeks) has been recommended since 2012 to protect newborns before they can be vaccinated themselves
Highly communicable: 80% secondary attack rate among susceptible household contacts
